questions.topic: Ch 7 · Fiscal functions · Musgrave's three functions
questions.stem: The three fiscal functions of government identified by Musgrave are:

options.explanation: These are activities of the economy, not the fiscal functions of government. Musgrave's classification is about the roles the budget plays.
These belong to monetary policy and the central bank, not to the fiscal (budgetary) functions of government.
Correct. Musgrave grouped the government's budgetary role into the allocation, distribution and stabilization functions.
These are instruments or methods of finance, not the three functions. The functions describe the purposes the budget serves.

questions.sourceRef: Musgrave's three fiscal functions: allocation, distribution, stabilization

questions.stem: Providing national defence and correcting pollution through the budget are examples of the government's:

options.explanation: Correct. The allocation function is about providing goods the market under-supplies and discouraging those it over-supplies, reallocating resources.
The distribution function is about reducing inequality of income and wealth, not about providing public goods or correcting externalities.
The stabilization function is about smoothing booms and slumps, controlling inflation and unemployment — not about the mix of goods provided.
Redemption is the repayment of public debt, not one of Musgrave's fiscal functions.

questions.sourceRef: Allocation function: provide public/merit goods, correct externalities

questions.stem: Levying higher tax rates on the rich and financing subsidies for the poor illustrates the:

options.explanation: The allocation function is about the mix of goods provided, not about redistributing income between groups.
Correct. Using progressive taxes and transfers to reduce inequality of income and wealth is the distribution (redistribution) function.
The stabilization function is about controlling inflation and unemployment over the business cycle, not about redistribution.
Monetary management belongs to the central bank, and is not one of Musgrave's fiscal functions.

questions.sourceRef: Distribution function: progressive taxes and transfers reduce inequality

questions.stem: Using the budget to restrain demand when prices are rising and to boost demand when unemployment is high is the:

options.explanation: The allocation function concerns which goods are provided, not the management of the overall level of demand over the cycle.
The distribution function concerns inequality of income, not the control of inflation and unemployment.
Correct. Smoothing the business cycle — restraining demand in a boom and boosting it in a slump — is the stabilization function.
Devolution is the sharing of taxes between the Centre and the States, not a fiscal function in Musgrave's sense.

questions.sourceRef: Stabilization function: smooth booms and slumps, control inflation and unemployment

questions.topic: Ch 7 · Fiscal functions · Matching the function
questions.stem: Which measure best illustrates the allocation function of government?

options.text: A cash transfer to families below the poverty line
options.explanation: This reduces inequality and so illustrates the distribution function, not allocation.

options.text: Raising public spending to pull the economy out of a recession
options.explanation: Boosting demand in a slump illustrates the stabilization function, not allocation.

options.text: Raising income-tax rates on the highest income slab
options.explanation: Taxing high incomes more heavily is aimed at redistribution — the distribution function, not allocation.

options.text: Building a public park that no private firm would supply
options.explanation: Correct. Providing a good the market under-supplies reallocates resources toward it — the allocation function.

questions.sourceRef: Allocation function providing a public good the market under-supplies

questions.topic: Ch 7 · Federal finance · Government in a mixed economy
questions.stem: In a mixed economy such as India, the government:

options.text: owns and runs every firm in the economy
options.explanation: That describes a fully planned or command economy, not a mixed economy where private firms do most of the producing.

options.text: performs the allocation, distribution and stabilization functions alongside private markets
options.explanation: Correct. In a mixed economy private markets do most production while the government carries out the three fiscal functions.

options.text: plays no role, leaving everything to the free market
options.explanation: That describes a pure market economy. A mixed economy has an active government role beside the market.

options.text: only prints money and sets interest rates
options.explanation: That is monetary policy alone; the government's role in a mixed economy is far wider, covering the fiscal functions.

readLink.label: Read: Government in a mixed economy, §2 →

questions.sourceRef: Mixed economy: private markets plus government performing the fiscal functions

questions.topic: Ch 7 · Federal finance · Centre and State powers
questions.stem: In India's federal structure, the power to tax and to spend is:

options.text: held entirely by the Central government
options.explanation: The States also have their own taxing and spending powers; the powers are not held by the Centre alone.

options.text: held entirely by the State governments
options.explanation: The Centre raises the larger national taxes and runs subjects of national reach, so the States do not hold the power alone.

options.text: divided between the Centre and the States
options.explanation: Correct. A federal structure splits taxing and spending powers between the Union and the States, each with its own subjects.

options.text: exercised only by local municipal bodies
options.explanation: Local bodies have limited powers; the primary division is between the Centre and the States.

questions.sourceRef: Federal finance: taxing and spending powers divided between Centre and States

questions.stem: The constitutional body that recommends how the shareable central taxes are divided between the Centre and the States is the:

options.explanation: The RBI conducts monetary policy and manages the currency; it does not recommend tax devolution between the Centre and the States.
Correct. The Finance Commission recommends the share of central taxes going to the States and how it is distributed among them (tax devolution).
The GST Council decides GST rates and administration; the sharing of the wider pool of central taxes is the Finance Commission's task.

options.text: Securities and Exchange Board of India
options.explanation: SEBI regulates securities markets and has nothing to do with tax devolution between the Centre and the States.

questions.sourceRef: Finance Commission recommends tax devolution between Centre and States

questions.stem: Market failure refers to a situation in which:

options.explanation: That is the opposite of market failure. Market failure is precisely the case where the market does not allocate efficiently.

options.text: the market, on its own, fails to allocate resources efficiently
options.explanation: Correct. Market failure means the price mechanism produces an inefficient allocation — the wrong quantities of goods.

options.text: the government takes over all production
options.explanation: Government takeover is a possible response, not the definition. Market failure describes an inefficient market outcome.

options.text: all prices in the economy fall to zero
options.explanation: Prices falling to zero is not what market failure means; the market still works but allocates resources inefficiently.

questions.sourceRef: Market failure = market fails to allocate resources efficiently

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a cause of market failure?

options.explanation: Public goods are a cause of market failure, because the free-rider problem leaves them under-supplied by the market.
Externalities are a cause of market failure, because private and social costs or benefits diverge.
Correct. Perfect competition delivers an efficient outcome, so it is not a cause of market failure; imperfect competition is.
Asymmetric information is a cause of market failure, because one side knowing more than the other distorts the market.

questions.sourceRef: Causes of market failure: public goods, externalities, imperfect competition, asymmetric information

questions.stem: A public good is characterised by being:

options.explanation: Correct. One person's use does not reduce what is left for others (non-rival), and non-payers cannot be shut out (non-excludable).
Rival and excludable describes a private good, not a public good.
This mixes the properties. A pure public good is both non-rival and non-excludable.
This mixes the properties. A pure public good is non-excludable as well as non-rival.

readLink.label: Read: Public, private and merit goods, §4 →

questions.sourceRef: Public good: non-rival and non-excludable

questions.stem: The free-rider problem arises because a public good is:

options.text: too expensive for the government to produce
options.explanation: Cost is not the source of the free-rider problem; non-excludability is.

options.text: non-excludable, so people can enjoy it without paying
options.explanation: Correct. Because non-payers cannot be shut out, each person hopes to enjoy the good for free, so the market under-provides it.
Public goods are non-rival, not rival; and rivalry is not the cause of the free-rider problem.

options.text: always provided by private firms at a profit
options.explanation: Private firms cannot profit from a non-excludable good, which is exactly why the free-rider problem leaves it to the government.

readLink.label: Read: Public, private and merit goods, §4 →

questions.sourceRef: Free-rider problem from non-excludability of public goods

questions.topic: Ch 7 · Public goods · Private good example
questions.stem: Which of the following is a pure private good?

options.explanation: National defence is non-rival and non-excludable — a public good, not a private good.
A streetlight is non-rival and non-excludable, so it is a public good, not a private good.
Correct. A meal is rival (one diner's meal is not another's) and excludable (no payment, no meal) — a private good.
A lighthouse beam is non-rival and non-excludable — the textbook public good, not a private good.

readLink.label: Read: Public, private and merit goods, §4 →

questions.sourceRef: Private good: rival and excludable

questions.stem: Education and healthcare, which society judges people should consume more of than they would choose to buy, are examples of:

options.explanation: Education and healthcare are usually excludable and rival, so they are not public goods, even though the government supports them.
An inferior good is one whose demand falls as income rises; that is unrelated to why the government promotes education and healthcare.
A Giffen good is a demand-theory curiosity; it has nothing to do with goods society thinks should be consumed more.
Correct. A merit good is one whose social benefit exceeds private demand, so the government encourages or subsidises it.

readLink.label: Read: Public, private and merit goods, §4 →

questions.sourceRef: Merit good: under-demanded relative to its social benefit

questions.stem: An externality is a cost or a benefit of an activity that:

options.text: falls on the buyer of the good only
options.explanation: A cost or benefit falling on the buyer is a private, internal effect, not an externality.

options.text: falls on the seller of the good only
options.explanation: A cost or benefit borne by the seller is a private, internal effect, not an externality.

options.text: falls on a third party and is not reflected in the market price
options.explanation: Correct. An externality spills over onto someone who is neither buyer nor seller, and the price does not capture it.

options.text: is always positive and benefits society
options.explanation: Externalities can be positive or negative; a polluting factory is a negative externality.

questions.sourceRef: Externality: third-party cost or benefit not reflected in the price

questions.stem: A factory that discharges untreated waste into a river creates a negative externality because:

options.text: social cost exceeds private cost, so the market over-produces the good
options.explanation: Correct. The clean-up cost falls on third parties, so social cost is above private cost and the firm, counting only its own cost, produces too much.

options.text: private cost exceeds social cost, so the market under-produces the good
options.explanation: For a negative externality social cost exceeds private cost, not the other way round, and the market over-produces.
That describes a positive externality, not the pollution case, which is about costs, not benefits.

options.text: there is no effect on any third party
options.explanation: The villagers downstream are third parties bearing the cost, which is exactly what makes it an externality.

questions.sourceRef: Negative externality: social cost > private cost, market over-produces

questions.stem: Because vaccination confers a positive externality, an unregulated market tends to:

options.explanation: Over-production is the result of a negative externality, not a positive one.
Correct. With a positive externality the social benefit exceeds the private benefit, so buyers counting only their private benefit take too little — the market under-produces.

options.text: produce exactly the socially efficient amount
options.explanation: The whole point of a positive externality is that the market misses the efficient amount, producing too little.
The good is still produced; it is simply produced in a smaller quantity than is socially efficient.

questions.sourceRef: Positive externality: social benefit > private benefit, market under-produces

questions.stem: A person smoking in a crowded public place, imposing fumes on those nearby, is best described as:

options.explanation: The effect is a harm, not a benefit, and it arises from consumption (the act of smoking), not production.
The fumes harm others, so the externality is negative, not positive.
The harm arises from an act of consumption, not from a firm's production process.
Correct. Smoking is an act of consumption that harms third parties, so it is a negative externality in consumption.

questions.sourceRef: Externalities in production and consumption; smoking = negative consumption externality

questions.stem: A monopoly causes market failure because, compared with perfect competition, it:

options.text: produces a larger output at a lower price
options.explanation: That describes perfect competition, not a monopoly. A monopoly does the opposite.

options.text: restricts output and charges a price above marginal cost
options.explanation: Correct. Market power lets the monopolist hold output back and set price above marginal cost, so some buyers who value the good above its cost go without — an inefficient outcome.
Zero long-run profit is a feature of perfect competition, not of a monopoly with market power.
A monopoly is about market power over a private good, not about supplying a public good.

questions.sourceRef: Monopoly restricts output and prices above marginal cost

questions.stem: A seller of a used car who knows its hidden faults while the buyer does not is an example of:

options.explanation: A used car is a private good; the issue here is unequal knowledge, not the properties of a public good.
There is no third-party benefit here; the problem is a gap in information between buyer and seller.
Correct. One party (the seller) knows more than the other (the buyer), which is the defining feature of asymmetric information.
A progressive tax is a taxation concept, unrelated to unequal knowledge between a buyer and a seller.

questions.sourceRef: Asymmetric information: one side knows more than the other

questions.stem: To correct a negative externality such as factory pollution, the government would typically:

options.text: impose a tax on the polluting activity
options.explanation: Correct. A tax makes the polluter bear the social cost, cutting output back toward the efficient level; regulation can do the same by rule.

options.text: pay a subsidy to the polluting activity
options.explanation: A subsidy would encourage more of the harmful activity, worsening the externality. Subsidies suit positive externalities.

options.text: provide the good free to everyone
options.explanation: Free provision suits a public good; it does not address the over-production caused by a negative externality.

options.text: ban all production in the whole economy
options.explanation: A blanket ban on all production is not a remedy; at most, targeted regulation of the harmful activity is used.

questions.sourceRef: Remedy: tax the negative externality (subsidise the positive one)

questions.stem: The government budget is best described as a statement of the government's:

options.text: estimated receipts and expenditure for a financial year
options.explanation: Correct. The budget sets out the estimated receipts and expenditure for the coming financial year, split into revenue and capital parts.

options.text: total stock of gold and foreign-exchange reserves
options.explanation: Reserves are held by the central bank; the budget is a statement of flows of receipts and spending, not a stock of reserves.
Those are monetary-policy variables set by the central bank, not the content of the government budget.

options.text: list of every private firm's profits
options.explanation: The budget concerns government receipts and spending, not the profits of private firms.

questions.sourceRef: Budget = statement of estimated receipts and expenditure for a year

questions.topic: Ch 7 · Budget · Revenue vs capital receipts
questions.stem: When the government borrows from the market, the money it receives is classified as a:

options.text: revenue receipt, because it adds to government funds
options.explanation: Adding to funds is not the test. Borrowing creates a liability, so it is a capital receipt, not a revenue receipt.

options.text: tax receipt, because it must be repaid
options.explanation: Borrowing is not a tax; a tax is a compulsory payment with no repayment. Borrowing is a capital receipt.

options.text: non-tax revenue receipt, like a fee
options.explanation: A fee is genuine revenue; borrowing is not, because it creates a liability, so it is a capital receipt.

options.text: capital receipt, because it creates a liability
options.explanation: Correct. Borrowing creates a liability the government must repay, so it is a capital receipt, never a revenue receipt.

questions.sourceRef: Borrowing creates a liability → capital receipt

questions.topic: Ch 7 · Revenue · Tax vs non-tax revenue
questions.stem: Which of the following is a source of NON-tax revenue for the government?

options.text: Licence and passport fees charged for a specific service
options.explanation: Correct. A fee is charged for a specific service the payer receives, so it is non-tax revenue, unlike a tax which has no direct service in return.
Income tax is a direct tax and so is tax revenue, not non-tax revenue.

options.text: Goods and Services Tax on goods
options.explanation: GST is an indirect tax and so is tax revenue, not non-tax revenue.
Corporation tax is a direct tax, and so counts as tax revenue rather than non-tax revenue.

questions.sourceRef: Non-tax revenue includes fees; a fee buys a specific service

questions.stem: The key difference between a direct tax and an indirect tax is that:

options.text: a direct tax is paid in cash and an indirect tax is paid in kind
options.explanation: The mode of payment is not the distinction; both are usually paid in money. The distinction is whether the burden can be shifted.

options.text: a direct tax is always larger than an indirect tax
options.explanation: Size is not the distinction. The point is whether the burden can be passed on to another person.

options.text: the burden of a direct tax cannot be shifted, while the burden of an indirect tax can be shifted
options.explanation: Correct. A direct tax is borne by the person who pays it; an indirect tax is levied on goods and its burden is passed on in the price.

options.text: only a direct tax is collected by the government
options.explanation: Both direct and indirect taxes are collected by the government; the distinction is the shifting of the burden.

questions.sourceRef: Direct tax: burden not shifted; indirect tax: burden shifted

questions.stem: A tax is described as progressive when:

options.text: the average rate of tax stays the same as income rises
options.explanation: A constant average rate describes a proportional tax, not a progressive one.

options.text: the average rate of tax rises as income rises
options.explanation: Correct. Under a progressive tax the average rate increases with income, so higher earners pay a larger share of their income.

options.text: the average rate of tax falls as income rises
options.explanation: A falling average rate describes a regressive tax, which bears more heavily on the poor.

options.text: everyone pays exactly the same amount of tax
options.explanation: A fixed amount for all is a lump-sum charge that is regressive in effect; it is not what makes a tax progressive.

questions.sourceRef: Progressive tax: average rate rises with income

questions.stem: Which of the following is one of Adam Smith's four canons of taxation?

options.text: Certainty — the amount, time and manner of payment should be clear to the taxpayer
options.explanation: Correct. Certainty is one of Adam Smith's four canons, alongside equality, convenience and economy.

options.text: Secrecy — the taxpayer should not know how the tax is calculated
options.explanation: This is the opposite of the canon of certainty, which requires the tax to be clear and not arbitrary.

options.text: Maximum yield at any cost of collection
options.explanation: This contradicts the canon of economy, which requires the cost of collection to be small relative to the revenue raised.

options.text: Inconvenience — payment at the time hardest for the taxpayer
options.explanation: This is the opposite of the canon of convenience, which requires payment at the time and manner most convenient for the taxpayer.

questions.sourceRef: Adam Smith's canons: equality, certainty, convenience, economy

questions.stem: The incidence of a tax refers to the person who:

options.text: first pays the tax to the government at the point of levy
options.explanation: That describes the impact of a tax, the initial burden, not the incidence.

options.text: designs the tax in the budget
options.explanation: The incidence is about who bears the tax, not who designs it.

options.text: collects the tax on the government's behalf
options.explanation: The collector is not necessarily the one who bears the tax; incidence is about the final burden.

options.text: finally bears the burden of the tax and cannot shift it further
options.explanation: Correct. Incidence is the final resting place of the burden — the person who cannot pass the tax on to anyone else.

questions.sourceRef: Impact = who pays first; incidence = who finally bears the tax

questions.topic: Ch 7 · Public debt · Internal vs external
questions.stem: The distinction between internal and external public debt is that:

options.text: internal debt is short-term and external debt is long-term
options.explanation: Maturity is not the dividing line. The distinction is whether the lender is inside or outside the country.

options.text: internal debt is interest-free and external debt carries interest
options.explanation: Both kinds normally carry interest. The distinction is the location of the lender, not the interest.

options.text: internal debt is owed to lenders within the country and external debt to lenders abroad
options.explanation: Correct. Internal debt is owed to domestic lenders and repaid in domestic currency; external debt is owed abroad and must be serviced in foreign currency.

options.text: internal debt need never be repaid but external debt must be
options.explanation: Both must be repaid (redeemed). The distinction is only the location of the lender.

questions.sourceRef: Internal debt owed within the country; external debt owed abroad

questions.stem: A person has a taxable income of ₹ 8,00,000 and pays income tax of ₹ 60,000. The average rate of tax is:

options.explanation: 6% would be ₹ 48,000 of tax, not ₹ 60,000. The average rate is tax divided by income.
12% would be ₹ 96,000 of tax. The correct figure is ₹ 60,000 ÷ ₹ 8,00,000.
Correct. Average tax rate = 60,000 ÷ 8,00,000 = 0.075, that is 7.5%.
8% would be ₹ 64,000 of tax. Dividing ₹ 60,000 by ₹ 8,00,000 gives 7.5%, not 8%.

questions.sourceRef: Average tax rate = tax ÷ income = 60,000 ÷ 8,00,000 = 7.5%

questions.stem: Under a slab system, income up to ₹ 2,50,000 is taxed at nil, income from ₹ 2,50,001 to ₹ 5,00,000 at 5%, and income from ₹ 5,00,001 to ₹ 10,00,000 at 20%. A person with a taxable income of ₹ 6,00,000 has a tax liability of:

options.explanation: ₹ 20,000 is only the 20% slab on the top ₹ 1,00,000; it omits the ₹ 12,500 charged on the 5% slab.
₹ 12,500 is only the 5% slab; it omits the ₹ 20,000 charged on the ₹ 1,00,000 in the 20% slab.
This wrongly applies 20% to the whole ₹ 6,00,000. A slab tax charges each rate only on the income within its band.

questions.sourceRef: Slab tax on 6,00,000: 5% of 2,50,000 + 20% of 1,00,000 = 32,500 (rates illustrative)

questions.stem: A proportional income tax charges every taxpayer 10% of income. Person A earns ₹ 3,00,000 and Person B earns ₹ 9,00,000. By how much more than A does B pay in tax?

options.explanation: Correct. B pays 10% of 9,00,000 = ₹ 90,000; A pays 10% of 3,00,000 = ₹ 30,000; the difference is ₹ 60,000.
₹ 30,000 is A's own tax, not the difference between B's tax and A's tax.
₹ 90,000 is B's total tax, not the amount by which it exceeds A's tax.
₹ 1,20,000 is the sum of the two taxes, not the difference between them.

questions.stem: For a year the government's revenue receipts are ₹ 1,600 crore and its revenue expenditure is ₹ 1,800 crore. The revenue deficit is:

options.explanation: ₹ 400 crore is not the gap here. Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts = 1,800 − 1,600.
Correct. Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts = 1,800 − 1,600 = ₹ 200 crore.
₹ 3,400 crore adds the two figures. The revenue deficit is the difference, not the sum.
The difference between 1,800 and 1,600 is 200, not 100.

questions.sourceRef: Revenue deficit = 1,800 − 1,600 = 200

questions.stem: A budget shows (₹ crore): revenue expenditure 2,300; capital expenditure 700; revenue receipts 2,000; non-debt capital receipts 200. The fiscal deficit is:

options.explanation: ₹ 600 crore ignores the non-debt capital receipts or miscounts the totals. Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − total receipts excluding borrowings.
₹ 1,000 crore would ignore the ₹ 200 crore of non-debt capital receipts. They must be added to revenue receipts before subtracting.
Correct. Total expenditure = 2,300 + 700 = 3,000; receipts excluding borrowings = 2,000 + 200 = 2,200; fiscal deficit = 3,000 − 2,200 = ₹ 800 crore.
₹ 400 crore is the revenue-account gap (2,300 − 2,000 minus something), not the fiscal deficit, which uses total expenditure and all non-borrowed receipts.

questions.sourceRef: Fiscal deficit = 3,000 − 2,200 = 800

questions.stem: The fiscal deficit of a government is ₹ 800 crore and its interest payments for the year are ₹ 400 crore. The primary deficit is:

options.explanation: ₹ 1,200 crore adds interest to the fiscal deficit. The primary deficit subtracts interest, not adds it.
₹ 800 crore is the fiscal deficit itself; the primary deficit removes interest payments from it.
₹ 200 crore is not the result of 800 − 400. The primary deficit is fiscal deficit minus interest = 800 − 400.
Correct. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments = 800 − 400 = ₹ 400 crore.

questions.sourceRef: Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest = 800 − 400 = 400

questions.stem: A government's total expenditure is ₹ 2,200 crore. Its revenue receipts are ₹ 1,600 crore and its non-debt capital receipts are ₹ 100 crore. The fiscal deficit is:

options.explanation: Correct. Receipts excluding borrowings = 1,600 + 100 = 1,700; fiscal deficit = 2,200 − 1,700 = ₹ 500 crore.
₹ 600 crore ignores the ₹ 100 crore of non-debt capital receipts, which must be added to revenue receipts.
₹ 700 crore subtracts only the revenue receipts and leaves out the non-debt capital receipts entirely.
₹ 2,100 crore subtracts only ₹ 100 crore from expenditure; all non-borrowed receipts (₹ 1,700 crore) must be subtracted.

questions.stem: If the fiscal deficit is ₹ 500 crore and interest payments are ₹ 300 crore, the primary deficit is:

options.explanation: ₹ 800 crore adds interest to the fiscal deficit. The primary deficit subtracts interest.
Correct. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments = 500 − 300 = ₹ 200 crore.
₹ 500 crore is the fiscal deficit itself; the primary deficit removes the ₹ 300 crore of interest.
₹ 300 crore is the interest figure, not the primary deficit, which is 500 − 300.

questions.sourceRef: Primary deficit = 500 − 300 = 200

questions.topic: Ch 7 · Deficits · Borrowing equals fiscal deficit
questions.stem: A government's total expenditure is ₹ 2,000 crore and its total receipts other than borrowings are ₹ 1,650 crore. The amount it must borrow this year is:

options.explanation: ₹ 1,650 crore is the non-borrowed receipts, not the borrowing. Borrowing equals the fiscal deficit, the gap that remains.
₹ 2,000 crore is the total expenditure; borrowing covers only the part not met by other receipts.
Correct. The fiscal deficit = 2,000 − 1,650 = ₹ 350 crore, and the fiscal deficit is exactly the amount borrowed.
₹ 3,650 crore adds expenditure and receipts. Borrowing is the difference, not the sum.

questions.sourceRef: Borrowing = fiscal deficit = 2,000 − 1,650 = 350

questions.stem: A government budgets total expenditure of ₹ 45,000 crore, revenue receipts of ₹ 32,000 crore and non-debt capital receipts of ₹ 3,000 crore. The fiscal deficit is:

options.explanation: ₹ 13,000 crore subtracts only the revenue receipts and ignores the ₹ 3,000 crore of non-debt capital receipts.
₹ 3,000 crore is the non-debt capital receipts figure, not the fiscal deficit.
₹ 35,000 crore is the total of non-borrowed receipts, not the deficit. The deficit is expenditure minus those receipts.
Correct. Receipts excluding borrowings = 32,000 + 3,000 = 35,000; fiscal deficit = 45,000 − 35,000 = ₹ 10,000 crore.

questions.stem: A government's revenue receipts are ₹ 2,500 crore and its revenue expenditure is ₹ 2,900 crore. The revenue deficit is:

options.explanation: Correct. Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts = 2,900 − 2,500 = ₹ 400 crore.
The difference between 2,900 and 2,500 is 400, not 600.
The difference between 2,900 and 2,500 is 400, not 200.
₹ 5,400 crore adds the two figures. The revenue deficit is the difference, not the sum.

questions.sourceRef: Revenue deficit = 2,900 − 2,500 = 400

questions.stem: A government reports a fiscal deficit of ₹ 5,60,000 crore and interest payments of ₹ 2,10,000 crore. Its primary deficit is:

options.explanation: ₹ 7,70,000 crore adds interest to the fiscal deficit. The primary deficit subtracts interest.
Correct. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments = 5,60,000 − 2,10,000 = ₹ 3,50,000 crore.
₹ 2,10,000 crore is the interest figure, not the primary deficit.
₹ 5,60,000 crore is the fiscal deficit itself; the primary deficit removes the interest payments.

questions.stem: Fiscal policy refers to the government's use of:

options.text: its taxation and expenditure (and borrowing) to influence the economy
options.explanation: Correct. Fiscal policy is the deliberate use of the budget — taxes, spending and borrowing — to influence output, employment and prices.

options.text: interest rates and the money supply set by the central bank
options.explanation: That is monetary policy, conducted by the central bank, not fiscal policy.

options.text: the exchange rate against foreign currencies
options.explanation: Exchange-rate management is a matter of external and monetary policy, not fiscal policy.

options.text: wage and price controls on private firms
options.explanation: Direct wage and price controls are not the instruments of fiscal policy, which works through taxes and public spending.

questions.sourceRef: Fiscal policy = government use of taxation and expenditure to influence the economy

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT normally listed as an objective of fiscal policy?

options.explanation: Economic growth is a standard objective of fiscal policy, so it is not the exception.
Full employment is a standard objective of fiscal policy, so it is not the exception.
Price stability is a standard objective of fiscal policy, so it is not the exception.

options.text: Maximising the profits of private firms
options.explanation: Correct. Fiscal policy aims at growth, employment, price stability and equity; maximising private-firm profits is not one of its objectives.

questions.sourceRef: Objectives: growth, employment, price stability, equity, stabilisation

questions.topic: Ch 7 · Fiscal policy · Fiscal vs monetary
questions.stem: Which of the following is an instrument of MONETARY policy rather than fiscal policy?

options.explanation: Changing tax rates is a fiscal-policy instrument, run through the budget, not monetary policy.

options.text: A change in the central bank's policy interest rate
options.explanation: Correct. The policy (repo) rate is a monetary-policy instrument set by the central bank, not a fiscal instrument.

options.text: A change in government spending on infrastructure
options.explanation: Public spending is a fiscal-policy instrument, not monetary policy.

options.text: A change in the size of the budget deficit
options.explanation: The budget deficit follows from the government's taxes and spending, so it is a fiscal matter, not monetary policy.

questions.sourceRef: Monetary policy uses interest rates and money supply; fiscal policy uses taxes and spending

questions.stem: The main instruments of fiscal policy are:

options.text: the repo rate, the reverse repo rate and the cash reserve ratio
options.explanation: These are monetary-policy instruments of the central bank, not fiscal-policy instruments.
These are monetary-policy tools, not the instruments of fiscal policy.

options.text: taxation, public expenditure, public debt and the budget
options.explanation: Correct. Fiscal policy works through taxation, public expenditure, public debt (borrowing) and the budget as a whole.
These are trade-policy tools; the instruments of fiscal policy are taxes, spending, borrowing and the budget.

questions.sourceRef: Instruments: taxation, public expenditure, public debt, the budget

questions.stem: To pull an economy out of a recession, an appropriate expansionary fiscal policy would be to:

options.text: cut taxes and raise public spending
options.explanation: Correct. Cutting taxes and raising spending both increase aggregate demand, which lifts output and employment in a recession; the deficit widens.

options.text: raise taxes and cut public spending
options.explanation: That is contractionary policy, which lowers aggregate demand and would deepen a recession.

options.text: raise taxes and raise public spending equally
options.explanation: This is not the standard expansionary prescription; the clear expansionary move is to cut taxes and raise spending.

options.text: keep the budget exactly balanced at all times
options.explanation: Insisting on a balanced budget prevents the deliberate stimulus a recession calls for.

questions.sourceRef: Expansionary fiscal policy: cut taxes, raise spending, widen deficit

questions.stem: During a period of high demand-pull inflation, a suitable contractionary fiscal policy would:

options.text: cut taxes to leave people with more to spend
options.explanation: Cutting taxes raises demand, which would worsen demand-pull inflation, not curb it.

options.text: increase public spending on new projects
options.explanation: Raising spending adds to demand and would fuel inflation, the opposite of what is needed.

options.text: print more money to fund the deficit
options.explanation: That is a monetary action and would tend to raise demand and inflation, not reduce it.

options.text: raise taxes and cut public spending to reduce aggregate demand
options.explanation: Correct. Raising taxes and cutting spending lower aggregate demand, cooling inflation; the deficit narrows or a surplus is built.

questions.sourceRef: Contractionary fiscal policy: raise taxes, cut spending, reduce demand

questions.stem: Which of the following is an automatic stabilizer?

options.text: A one-off tax cut announced in the Budget speech
options.explanation: A deliberately announced tax cut is discretionary policy, not an automatic stabilizer.

options.text: A progressive income tax that yields less as incomes fall in a slump
options.explanation: Correct. A progressive tax takes less automatically as incomes drop, cushioning demand with no new decision — a classic automatic stabilizer.

options.text: A new highway project approved by the cabinet
options.explanation: A newly approved spending project is discretionary policy, requiring a fresh decision, not an automatic stabilizer.

options.text: A change in the central bank's repo rate
options.explanation: The repo rate is a monetary-policy tool, not a fiscal automatic stabilizer.

questions.sourceRef: Automatic stabilizer: progressive tax and unemployment benefit act with no new decision

questions.stem: Discretionary fiscal policy differs from an automatic stabilizer in that discretionary policy:

options.text: works without any deliberate decision by the government
options.explanation: Working without a decision describes an automatic stabilizer, not discretionary policy.

options.text: is conducted only by the central bank
options.explanation: The central bank conducts monetary policy; discretionary fiscal policy is decided by the government.
Discretionary policy is about deliberate tax and spending changes generally, not only to public goods.

options.text: requires a deliberate, announced change in taxes or spending
options.explanation: Correct. Discretionary policy is a deliberate, legislated change, whereas an automatic stabilizer reacts on its own with no new decision.

questions.sourceRef: Discretionary policy: deliberate, announced change in taxes or spending

questions.topic: Ch 7 · Fiscal policy · Effect on aggregate demand
questions.stem: A rise in government spending, other things equal, affects aggregate demand by:

options.text: reducing it, because the government competes with private buyers
options.explanation: Government spending is itself part of aggregate demand, so a rise adds to it rather than reducing it.

options.text: leaving it unchanged, since spending only moves money around
options.explanation: Government spending is a direct component of aggregate demand, so raising it increases total demand.

options.text: raising it, because government spending is a component of aggregate demand
options.explanation: Correct. Government spending is one of the components of aggregate demand, so a rise in it directly increases total spending in the economy.

options.text: raising it only if taxes are raised by the same amount
options.explanation: A rise in spending raises aggregate demand directly; it does not depend on a matching tax rise, which would work in the opposite direction.

questions.sourceRef: Government spending is a component of aggregate demand; a rise increases it
